title: Analysis of the Quality of Stuttering Content on Douyin in China
screen_reason: Abstract-only, but the abstract itself carries a complete CONTENT prevalence estimate with its denominator: 100 top-liked stuttering-related Douyin videos (12-15 May 2024) were classified as Useful, Personal experience or Misleading, and 74% were classified as Misleading. This is explicit misleading-coding of items, not a quality instrument (the PEMAT-A/V scores reported alongside are separate and are not extracted). The authors describe the result as 'the prevalence of misinformation about stuttering on Chinese new media platforms'. What the abstract does NOT give is who coded, against what standard, or any reliability statistic, which is reflected in ground_truth_detail and confidence.

estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 top-liked stuttering-related Douyin videos classified as Misleading
estimates.value_raw: 74% classified as misleading (74 of 100 videos); the other categories were useful 4% and personal experience 22%
estimates.denominator: 100 top-liked stuttering-related videos on Douyin, collected 12-15 May 2024
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if it was placed in the 'Misleading (M)' category of a three-way classification (Useful / Personal experience / Misleading). The abstract does not state the criteria used to judge a video misleading, nor the professional background of the raters.
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition is given in the abstract; the operational scheme is "The videos were classified into three categories as follows: Useful (U), Personal experience (P) and Misleading (M)", and the conclusion refers to "the prevalent misinformation" and "unreliable stuttering-related content".
estimates.source_quote: Through review and analysis, we found that 4% of the videos was classified as useful, 22% was classified as personal experience, and 74% was classified as misleading.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NOT REPORTED in the available text. The abstract states only that the videos were 'reviewed and analysed' and classified into Useful / Personal experience / Misleading; it names no coders, no external standard (no fact-check source, no clinical guideline), and no inter-rater reliability statistic. Coded researcher_coding by elimination, since no fact-checker, domain list, crowd or classifier is mentioned. The Background notes that untrained 'stuttering correctionists' spread misinformation about stuttering in China (Ma et al. 2023), suggesting a clinical/professional standard, but that is context rather than a stated method.
estimates.moderator_quote: A sample of 100 top-liked stuttering-related videos was collected between 12 and 15 May 2024.
estimates.notes: The value itself is unambiguous and verbatim (74% of exactly 100 videos, so the count is 74), which is why this is extractable from an abstract at all. Confidence is capped at medium, not high, because the coding procedure is invisible: no criteria, no rater qualifications, no reliability. borderline=false because 'Misleading' is an explicit misleading label applied item by item, which §3 admits as CONTENT, and because 'Personal experience' is a separate category, so the misleading bucket is not absorbing mere anecdote or incompleteness - though with the full text one could check whether unsupported personal claims were pushed into M. denom_scope=topical with denom_selection=curated: a single-topic corpus, rank-truncated to the 100 most-LIKED videos, which is a popularity-biased frame and the abstract notes 'Misleading videos are more likely to be liked by viewers' - so this 74% is very likely above the rate in an unweighted sample of stuttering videos. Douyin mapped to platform_norm TikTok (its international twin); if this project keeps Douyin distinct, that is the one field to change.

missed_or_uncertain: The text is an ABSTRACT ONLY, so anything not in the abstract is unavailable: no methods detail on the search terms, no coder count or qualifications, no reliability statistic, no table of per-category counts, and no figures. Not extracted from what is available: (a) the PEMAT-A/V results - average understandability 53.0% and average actionability 24.3%, described as low on both - these are QUALITY scale scores (means of a patient-education instrument), not shares of misinformation, so no prevalence row; (b) 'Useful' 4% and 'Personal experience' 22%, the complement categories of the row kept; a broader numerator (misleading plus unverified personal experience = 96%) would be a cross-category sum I computed and is barred by R8; (c) 'Misleading videos are more likely to be liked by viewers' - stated with no numbers, no correlation coefficient and no test, so nothing to extract; (d) the Background's reference to Ma et al. (2023) on untrained 'stuttering correctionists' spreading misinformation - a claim cited from another paper, barred by R8. Flag for the adjudicator: if the full text becomes available it should be checked for (i) the definition of the Misleading category and the ground truth it was judged against, (ii) whether more than one rater coded and any kappa, and (iii) the search keywords and how 'top-liked' was operationalised - all three could move breadth, ground_truth_detail and confidence, though none should move the 74% itself.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a popularity-ranked sample, reported from the abstract only. Sampling frame: 100 top-liked stuttering-related Douyin videos collected over a four-day window, 12-15 May 2024; the search terms, the exclusion criteria and the total pool from which the top 100 were drawn are not reported. Classification: a three-category scheme (Useful, Personal experience, Misleading) plus four extracted video features, with the PEMAT-A/V used for comprehensibility and actionability percentiles. Coding procedure: not reported - no number of raters, no rater expertise, no blinding, no external ground-truth standard and NO inter-rater reliability statistic appears in the abstract. No human participants, so no response rate; no ethics statement visible. The popularity-ranked frame is the main design threat to the estimate, and the authors' own observation that misleading videos attract more likes means the sampling mechanism is correlated with the outcome, biasing the 74% upward relative to a random sample of stuttering content.
rob.item6_quote: The videos were classified into three categories as follows: Useful (U), Personal experience (P) and Misleading (M), and four features were extracted for analysis.
rob.item10_quote: Through review and analysis, we found that 4% of the videos was classified as useful, 22% was classified as personal experience, and 74% was classified as misleading.
